task.goal: Make a nonprofit's public FAQ easier to update when policy answers change.
hard_constraints: One editor has two hours weekly and a static website; no new content system.
Do not publish an answer without a named source and review date.
Track stale answers, conflicting pages and reader failures to find a current answer.
task.available_resources: Existing FAQ files and policy memo archive.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One canonical answer per policy question
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make each policy answer live in exactly one existing static FAQ location. Replace repeated answers elsewhere with descriptive links to that location. This changes the maintenance problem: a policy revision requires one substantive edit instead of several synchronized edits.

For every answer, show the named source document, its archive identifier or date, and the date the editor checked the answer against it. A scheduled next-review date can also support maintenance. If the archive does not support an answer, publish only a notice that the answer is awaiting verification, with a contact route; do not infer policy.

Keep a small spreadsheet or text register beside the existing files: question, canonical URL, source, review date, next review, and known pages that repeat or contradict it. Add a visible “Couldn’t find a current answer?” email link using an existing monitored address. Record the reader’s question and starting page, without retaining unnecessary personal details.

Use the weekly two hours for 20 minutes reviewing new memos and reader reports, 70 minutes updating affected canonical answers and removing conflicting copies, and 30 minutes checking overdue entries and links. Begin with the most frequently changing questions; record remaining duplication as an explicit backlog.

This assumes the editor can edit relevant static pages and access a monitored inbox. External copies remain outside direct control. Links may also make readers take an extra step, so descriptive link wording matters.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot five questions with known repetition. Compare updating one changed policy through canonical answers against the current duplicate-edit process, recording time and missed contradictions. Ask three unfamiliar readers to locate the current answer from different starting pages and identify its source and review date. Inspect the register for overdue answers and unresolved conflicts. The mechanism fails its initial check if duplication remains unnoticed or readers cannot reliably reach the canonical answer.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Trace policy changes to affected answers
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep the FAQ’s current structure, but maintain a lightweight dependency register connecting policy memos to every public passage they support. The primary mechanism is change propagation: when a memo changes, the register supplies a concrete checklist of affected answers and potentially conflicting pages.

Use a spreadsheet or plain text file with one row per answer or policy-bearing passage: page location, question, named source and specific section, last review date, next review date, and status. Each published answer also displays its named source and last review date. A new or revised memo triggers review of all linked rows. Search the existing website files for distinctive terms and old wording to catch passages missing from the register. Record contradictory pages until corrected; record unsupported answers for removal or replacement with an awaiting-verification notice.

Spend 25 minutes weekly inspecting archive additions, 65 minutes applying the highest-impact changes, and 30 minutes checking overdue rows, unresolved conflicts, and reader reports. Add a plain email feedback link asking what answer the reader sought and where they looked; log unresolved searches in the same register. Those reports trigger dependency and navigation checks.

This uses the existing files and memo archive without changing publishing infrastructure. It assumes archive changes can be identified and sources are sufficiently specific to map to answers. Initial mapping takes time, so inventory a manageable section each week and mark unmapped sections explicitly. The largest uncertainty is whether the register can stay complete within the editor’s time budget.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Map one FAQ section, then select an archived policy revision whose affected passages can be independently inspected. Compare register-guided review with a simple keyword search of the same files. Count affected passages missed and minutes required, without assuming either method is complete. Submit one simulated failed-search report and verify that it enters the register and leads to a concrete check. Reject or simplify this approach if maintaining dependencies consumes more time than it saves or repeatedly misses relevant pages.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Time-limited answers with a weekly renewal queue
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Give every answer a defined period of validity for publication, then use a weekly renewal queue to prevent unsupported answers from remaining indefinitely. The mechanism is a publication gate: an answer stays available as current guidance only while its documented review remains within its assigned interval.

Add a named source, last review date, and next review date to each answer. Use shorter intervals for policies known to change frequently and longer intervals for stable material; choose initial intervals provisionally because the archive may not establish change frequency. Maintain a plain register sorted by next review date, with columns for conflicting pages and reader failures. Every weekly session also checks new policy memos, which can trigger immediate review before an answer’s scheduled date.

Allocate 20 minutes to new memos and reader feedback, 75 minutes to renewing or replacing due answers, and 25 minutes to finding contradictory wording and updating the register. If an answer cannot be verified, replace its substantive guidance with a clear verification-pending notice and an existing contact route. A visible email link collects reports of missing, confusing, or apparently outdated answers. Log these reports even when the answer is technically current.

This requires only edits to static files and a small register. It assumes the editor can sustain weekly publication and that a contact route already exists. Expiration is handled manually, so missed sessions remain a risk. Review intervals cannot guarantee correctness between checks, and withdrawing answers can reduce usefulness; track pending notices as a backlog, not as successful maintenance.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot a small FAQ section for four weekly sessions, using intervals short enough to exercise renewal. Compare it with a similar section maintained by the existing routine. Inspect overdue published answers, editing time, conflicting passages, and questions left without useful guidance. Ask three readers to distinguish current guidance from a pending notice and find the contact route. The approach fails if renewals exceed the available time, overdue answers remain presented as current, or withdrawals create more unresolved reader failures than the workflow can address.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use source excerpts to reduce policy rewriting
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Replace selected paraphrased FAQ answers with short, exact excerpts from the policy memo archive, preceded by a plain-language question and a brief statement of who and what the excerpt covers. The primary mechanism is reducing translation work: the editor selects and checks authoritative wording instead of repeatedly reconstructing policy explanations. Keep existing static files and navigation; no new publishing system is required.

Every published answer must display the named source memo, its date and section, and the date the editor reviewed it. Include any conditions or exceptions needed to make the excerpt accurate. If the archive does not establish which conflicting memo governs, replace the substantive answer with a verification-pending notice rather than choosing a policy interpretation.

Keep a plain-text work log alongside the FAQ files. Record each answer’s location, source, review date, next check, and unresolved issues under three labels: stale answer, conflicting page, and reader could not find current guidance. Add an email feedback link using an existing monitored address, asking which question the reader sought and where they looked. Search existing site files for wording from superseded excerpts and related terms whenever a policy changes; log conflicting passages until resolved.

Budget the weekly two hours as 20 minutes checking archive changes and feedback, 70 minutes replacing affected excerpts and correcting conflicting pages, and 30 minutes checking stale entries and reader navigation failures. Start with a small section and expand within that allowance.

This assumes the editor can identify authoritative memos, quote them publicly, and access an existing feedback inbox. It works best when memo passages are short and understandable. Dense, confidential, or interdependent policies may make excerpts unsuitable; their readability and completeness remain unproven.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Prototype three excerpt-based answers and compare them with three manually checked paraphrases covering the same policies, all carrying sources and review dates. Use one archived revision to rehearse an update; record editing time, omitted conditions, and remaining contradictory passages. Ask three unfamiliar readers to find an answer and apply it to a scenario involving an exception. Log a simulated failed-search report and an intentionally overdue review. Reject the approach if excerpts save no editing time, obscure policy conditions, or prevent readers from identifying applicable current guidance.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Maintain policy answers as explicit decision tables
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
For policies whose answers depend on eligibility, dates, or exceptions, replace branching FAQ prose with small decision tables in the existing static pages. Each row states a reader’s circumstances, the applicable answer, and any exception. The mechanism is making policy branches explicit: a change to one eligibility condition becomes a bounded row edit, while overlapping or missing cases become easier to inspect. This could reduce the effort of checking prose that scatters conditions across several answers.

Use the existing memo archive to build one table at a time. Every substantive row must display its named source memo and section plus the date the editor reviewed it. Include effective dates where relevant. Publish a row only when its conditions and answer are supported; unresolved cases receive a verification-pending notice without speculative guidance. Use ordinary HTML tables with clear headers and short introductory instructions; no new content system or generator is needed.

Keep a plain-text issue list beside the files with three categories: stale rows, conflicting pages, and readers unable to find current guidance. Record the affected location, discovery date, and next action. When editing a table, search existing files for the changed condition and previous answer, and log contradictions until corrected. Add a feedback email link if an existing monitored address is available; otherwise, reader checks during the weekly session supply failure reports.

Reserve 20 minutes weekly for new memos and reports, 70 for table updates and conflicting pages, and 30 for overdue reviews and one reader-path check. Initial conversion must fit that same allowance, starting with one small policy family.

This assumes policies can be expressed as a manageable set of cases. Interacting conditions can make tables unwieldy, and a complete-looking table can conceal missing cases. Source interpretation and accessibility still require judgment.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Prototype one table for a policy with an exception. Compare it with the existing prose after checking both against the same memos. Rehearse one archived policy change and record editing time and missed affected passages. Ask three readers to find and apply guidance for an ordinary case, an exception, and an unsupported case. Inspect source and review-date coverage, and log any failed lookup. Reject the approach for that policy if it takes longer to maintain without improving case accuracy, or if readers confidently choose incorrect rows.

EXPAND.title: Answer with bounded policy excerpts
EXPAND.proposal:
Use short, exact policy excerpts as the substantive answer where a memo directly answers the question. This reduces the interpretation and rewriting needed after policy changes. Compared with the prior dependency-register route, it addresses a different weakness: finding every affected page does not prevent an editor from introducing errors while paraphrasing policy.

The editor first pilots one small FAQ section, identifying the memo passage supporting each answer. Publish the question, a short quotation with its relevant conditions and exceptions, the named memo and section, and the date checked. Add plain-language context only when the source directly supports it. The archive must establish which memo governs; a newer date alone does not settle conflicting authority.

Each weekly session uses 25 minutes to inspect archive changes, 65 minutes to replace affected excerpts and search existing website files for superseded wording, and 30 minutes to inspect unresolved issues. Keep a plain issue file recording stale answers, contradictory pages, and reader failures reported through an existing contact route. Reports can also be recorded manually from existing correspondence; no new inbox or service is required.

If a passage requires interpretation, omits an essential exception, or conflicts with another apparently applicable memo, replace the substantive answer with a verification-pending notice. Record the specific uncertainty for whoever already owns the policy; if no such person is available, leave it pending. Retain the previous file locally for recovery, but do not restore guidance known to be unsupported.

This needs only static-file editing and archive access. It assumes some memos contain readable, publicly shareable answers. Legalistic wording, confidential source material, and policies spread across several documents can make the approach unsuitable.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor trials four questions within one two-hour session. Draft each using excerpts and, separately, the prior register-guided paraphrase approach. Inspect both against the same source passages, counting omitted conditions and editing minutes. Ask two available readers to explain the resulting guidance and record misunderstandings. Stop expansion if excerpts do not reduce editing effort or source mismatches, or if they increase comprehension failures. Unsupported or ambiguous examples remain pending in both versions.

EXPAND.title: Publish policy revisions as complete change packets
EXPAND.proposal:
Treat each policy revision as one small release that must be complete before publication. The mechanism prevents partially updated websites: individually correct edits can still leave conflicting answers when published separately.

The editor creates a plain text packet for one revised policy. It contains the named governing memo, affected questions, website search terms, every located conflicting passage, proposed replacements, and a completion checklist. Search existing files for old wording and related terms; record uncertain matches explicitly. Every replacement answer includes its named source and review date. Prepare the edits in local copies, then inspect the complete set before using the website's existing publishing method.

Use 20 minutes weekly to identify revisions and reader reports, 75 minutes to prepare and publish the highest-priority packet, and 25 minutes to inspect the public pages and issue backlog. Work on only one packet at a time. Keep stale answers, unresolved contradictions, and failed reader searches in a small issue file, including reports that are unrelated to the active packet.

If the packet cannot be completed within the session, save the draft. Where existing public guidance is known to be unsupported, replace it with a verification-pending notice rather than leaving it presented as current. If publishing cannot update files together, temporarily withdraw the affected substantive answers, upload the complete changes, and check them immediately. Recover from upload failure using the pending notices; restore old guidance only if it remains supported.

This uses existing files, the archive, and local draft copies. It assumes the editor can publish all affected pages. It cannot guarantee that discovery found every duplicate, and withdrawal may temporarily reduce usefulness. Its distinctive benefit is controlling the transition between policy versions, rather than maintaining a permanent dependency map.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor replays one archived revision on local copies, comparing a change packet with ordinary page-by-page editing. Interrupt each after the same elapsed time and inspect how many contradictory or unsupported answers would be public, then finish and measure total minutes and temporary withdrawals. Stop after this single revision if packet preparation exceeds two hours, fails to reduce inconsistent publication states, or causes more unavailable guidance without a corresponding reduction in contradictions. Do not publish the historical policy during the trial.

EXPAND.title: Maintain concrete reader cases as policy regression checks
EXPAND.proposal:
Maintain a small set of concrete reader situations alongside the static FAQ. After a policy revision, use those situations to check whether the website still leads readers to a supported answer. The mechanism detects problems through observable answers to real questions, including contradictions that do not share recognizable wording with the revised memo.

Start with six situations drawn from existing FAQ questions: for example, a reader with a particular eligibility condition asking what they should do next. For each, record the starting page, question, expected answer supported by a named memo and section, and review date. These are maintenance checks in a plain text file, not new public policy or a content system.

Allocate 25 minutes weekly to inspect new memos and update affected expected answers from the sources. Spend 65 minutes walking the cases through the public pages and correcting failures, then 30 minutes inspecting overdue source checks and the issue log. Every published answer must display its named source and review date. Log stale answers, conflicting pages encountered during a case, and failures to locate current guidance. Reader questions received through an existing contact route can replace low-value cases, keeping the set small.

If the source cannot establish an expected answer, mark the case unresolved and replace affected unsupported guidance with a verification-pending notice. Record the policy question for an existing policy owner if one is available. After edits, repeat the failed case and inspect any linked contradictory page before closing the issue.

This assumes the FAQ and archive provide enough detail for concrete situations. It requires no software beyond text editing and a browser. Coverage is deliberately limited: rare questions can escape the cases, and the editor's familiarity can hide navigation problems. Keep unchecked sections visible in the log rather than treating passing cases as proof that the whole FAQ is current.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor trials six cases on one FAQ section within two hours, comparing the resulting issue list with an equal-time keyword review of that section. Verify each reported defect against the archive; count valid stale or conflicting answers found, current-answer retrieval failures, and maintenance minutes. If an unfamiliar reader is available, have them attempt two cases to expose editor familiarity. Stop expansion if case upkeep displaces actual corrections or finds no additional actionable failures over the simpler review. Retain any verified issues regardless of which method found them.

EXPAND.title: Improved P1: Trace policy changes to affected answers
EXPAND.proposal:
Retain P1’s dependency-register mechanism: connect source memos to the public passages they support so a policy change produces an editing checklist. The substantive improvement is explicit coverage accounting and a fallback when memo changes cannot be reliably identified. P1’s register could otherwise look complete while missing unexamined pages or archive revisions.

Use a plain text table containing each FAQ location, named source and section, review date, next review date, and coverage status: verified, unresolved, or not yet inspected. Display the named source and review date on every published answer. During initial inspection, withdraw substantive answers lacking either requirement and leave a verification-pending notice. Include known conflicting pages and reader failures in the same file, recording where readers started and what they sought through existing correspondence, if available.

The editor owns a two-hour weekly session: 25 minutes checking archive changes, 65 minutes updating affected passages, and 30 minutes checking overdue entries, conflicts, and publication results. Search website files for related terms as well as registered passages. Close an issue only after inspecting the public result and its known conflicting locations.

This requires file editing, archive access, and an identifiable governing source. A newer memo alone does not establish authority. Unresolved authority goes to an existing policy owner if available; otherwise guidance stays pending. If archive changes cannot be identified, use the same register for a rotating source recheck, starting with overdue and reported answers. Record the resulting detection delay. If initial inventory exceeds capacity, inspect one section weekly and preserve the visible uninspected backlog.
EXPAND.experiment: For two weekly sessions, the editor compares this version with ordinary P1 on two similarly sized FAQ sections. Record editing time, answers missed by the initial dependency list, unsupported public answers, and unresolved reader searches. Finish each session with a file search and public-page inspection. Stop expanding the register if maintenance consumes the session without correcting the highest-priority issue. No missed answers found, with greater bookkeeping time and no improvement in completed corrections, would show no demonstrated gain over P1.

EXPAND.title: Route reader language through a static question index
EXPAND.proposal:
Make discovery easier through a small static index of reader phrases that link to existing FAQ answers. The primary mechanism is vocabulary translation: several ways of asking a question can reach the same answer without adding policy wording to each entry. This targets failed discovery and the maintenance burden created when editors respond by publishing another answer page.

The editor starts with one FAQ section. Extract alternative phrases from existing FAQ headings and, where available, reader correspondence. Add a plain HTML list organized by reader task, with descriptive links and stable page anchors. Index entries contain questions or task labels only; eligibility rules, deadlines, and exceptions remain in the answers. The route works with existing answer locations and does not require first consolidating the website.

Before linking an answer, verify its named source and display its review date. Unsupported answers receive a verification-pending notice. Keep a plain issue file recording overdue reviews, contradictory pages, and reader questions that failed to reach current guidance. Known contradictions must be resolved or their unsupported guidance withdrawn; improving navigation alone does not resolve them.

Each weekly session reserves 25 minutes for archive changes and reports, 65 minutes for answer corrections, and 30 minutes for index repairs, overdue checks, and public-link inspection. When a policy changes, update the affected answers and inspect index labels for misleading promises. When a search fails, add or revise a reader phrase only if an existing verified answer actually addresses it; otherwise record an answer gap.

This needs only static-file editing and the memo archive. Useful reader language may be unavailable initially, so begin with existing questions and mark labels provisional. If an anchor cannot be maintained, link to the page with its exact heading. If no source-supported answer exists, route to a clearly labeled pending item rather than an unrelated answer.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor trials one section for two weeks, comparing the index with its existing FAQ entry page using six realistic questions. Where willing readers are available, alternate starting pages and observe whether they find a current, applicable answer; otherwise use an explicitly limited editorial walkthrough. Record failures, wrong-answer selections, clicks, and index upkeep time. Stop adding labels if they introduce wrong-answer selections or displace necessary policy corrections. Equal discovery success with additional upkeep would show no gain; editorial results alone cannot establish reader usability.
